problem: 'Torsion measures how fast the curve leaves its own plane' is loose: a space curve has no single 'own plane'. Torsion is the rate at which the osculating plane (the plane of T and N) turns about the tangent, per unit arc length. A student may read this as distance from a fixed plane.
fix: Say: 'Torsion measures how fast the osculating plane — the plane containing T and N — turns as you move along the curve, per unit arc length.'

problem: The claim 'Its derivative dT/ds is perpendicular to T' is stated with no reason. Students memorise it but cannot reproduce the one-line proof.
fix: Add: because |T| = 1 is constant, T · T = 1; differentiating gives 2T · (dT/ds) = 0, so dT/ds ⊥ T.

problem: N = (dT/ds)/|dT/ds| is undefined where dT/ds = 0 (κ = 0, e.g. a straight line or at an inflection). The chapter defines N without saying this, so students think N always exists.
fix: Add: 'This definition needs κ ≠ 0; at a point where κ = 0 the principal normal is not defined and the frame breaks down.'

problem: In the torsion formula note, 'the dot is the scalar triple product' mislabels the operation. The dot is the dot product; the whole combination (r′ × r″) · r‴ is the scalar triple product.
fix: Write: 'the whole numerator (r′ × r″) · r‴ is the scalar triple product of r′, r″ and r‴.'

problem: 'Swapping the order in (r′ × r″) · r‴ flips the sign of τ' is ambiguous. A cyclic swap r′ → r″ → r‴ leaves the triple product unchanged; only an odd swap (one interchange, e.g. r″ × r′) flips the sign.
fix: Say: 'interchanging two of the three vectors — for example writing (r″ × r′) · r‴ instead of (r′ × r″) · r‴ — flips the sign of τ; a cyclic reordering does not.'

problem: The answer gives |r′| = 5 without units, although Q2 has just asked about units and the coordinates are in metres.
fix: Answer: r′ = (−3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4); |r′| = √(9 sin²t + 9 cos²t + 16) = √25 = 5 m.

problem: The chapter never says τ can be negative or what the sign means, although the formula itself produces signs. Students then assume torsion is always a positive number like curvature.
fix: Add: 'κ is never negative, but τ carries a sign. Positive τ and negative τ correspond to the two opposite senses of twisting (right-handed and left-handed helices); the magnitude |τ| is the turning rate of the plane.'
